name: Kalimpong, Lava & Lolegaon
tagline: Wool-trade town, Lepcha ridges and red panda forest
meta_description: Kalimpong, Lava, Lolegaon and the Pedong villages on a fair budget: monasteries, nurseries, Neora Valley, Teesta rafting and homestays from ₹1,300 with meals.
summary: Kalimpong sits at 1,247 m, about 70 km above Siliguri, on a ridge over the Teesta. Come for its monasteries, haat and nurseries, then go east to Lava, Lolegaon and Neora Valley's forests, or to the homestay villages round Pedong. Quieter and cheaper than Darjeeling: ₹1,300–4,000 a day.

story.title: From Bhutan's hills to the wool road to Lhasa
paras: The first people of these hills were the Lepcha, who call themselves Rongkup. In the late 17th century the Lepcha chief Gaeboo Achyok held a principality from his fort at Damsang, above Pedong, and fought the Bhutanese for these ridges. Bhutan won, executed him and ruled the hills east of the Teesta for more than 150 years; the Bhutanese built Thongsa Gompa in Kalimpong in 1692. Every 20 December the Lepcha community still gathers at the ruins of Damsang to remember Achyok.

The Anglo-Bhutan war of 1864–65 ended with the Treaty of Sinchula, signed in November 1865, which gave the British the Bhutanese land east of the Teesta. In 1866 Kalimpong joined Darjeeling district. Scottish missionaries came in the 1870s, and in 1900 the Rev. Dr John Anderson Graham opened the homes for Anglo-Indian children that are now Dr Graham's Homes on Deolo. Meanwhile mule caravans came down from Lhasa over Jelep La, through Pedong, and Kalimpong became India's main market for Tibetan wool.

The 1962 war closed Jelep La, and the trade ended almost overnight. Kalimpong turned to schools, flower nurseries and visitors. Tibetans who had fled after 1959 rebuilt monasteries here, among them Zang Dhok Palri on Durpin, consecrated by the 14th Dalai Lama in 1976. To the east, the forest department built lodges at Lava and Lolegaon, and Neora Valley became a national park in 1986. In February 2017 Kalimpong became a district of its own.

intro: Kalimpong is a working hill town of schools, nurseries, monasteries and a twice-weekly haat, on a saddle between Deolo and Durpin hills at about 1,247 m. Most people give it a night on the way to Gangtok. We think it deserves two or three, and the villages around it deserve more: this is the land for slow travel in homestays, with Kanchenjunga on the skyline from October to May.

East of town the road climbs through Algarah to Lava, a monastery village at 2,195 m on the edge of Neora Valley National Park, one of the last strongholds of the red panda in Bengal. Beyond are Kolakham and Rishyap on forest ridges, and Lolegaon and Charkhole among old cypress and pine. North-east lies Pedong on the old Tibet road, with Sillery Gaon, Icchey Gaon and Ramdhura in the hills around it. Down at the river, Teesta Bazar has rafting in season.

It is a cheap land to travel well. Homestays charge ₹1,300–2,200 per person with dinner and breakfast, and forest and tourism lodges are fairly priced. The catch is transport: shared jeeps serve the town and Pedong well, but the forest villages need cars. And NH10, the main road up the Teesta, has had long closures since the October 2023 flood, so build in a spare day.

highlights.title: Zang Dhok Palri on Durpin
highlights.text: The Tibetan monastery on Durpin hill, 1,372 m, was established in 1957 by Dudjom Rinpoche and consecrated by the 14th Dalai Lama in 1976. It holds the 108 volumes of the Kangyur, and on clear mornings the terrace looks across the Teesta to the Kanchenjunga range.

highlights.title: Haat day and Kalimpong cheese
highlights.text: On Wednesdays and Saturdays villagers bring squash shoots, ferns, churpi, baskets and fruit to the haat near the Motor Stand. Then find Kalimpong cheese and milk lollipops, first made at Father André Butty's Swiss Welfare Dairy, which closed in 1990.

highlights.title: Red pandas of Neora Valley
highlights.text: Neora Valley National Park, declared in 1986, climbs from about 183 m to 3,200 m east of Lava. Guided day trips to Rachela and Mouchuki go from Lava with a forest department permit. The park closes from mid-June to mid-September.

highlights.title: Old forests of Lolegaon
highlights.text: Lolegaon's heritage forest has a canopy walk through tall cypress and pine, and the Jhandi Dara viewpoint gives a sunrise on Kanchenjunga. Charkhole and Rishyap nearby have similar views with far fewer people.

highlights.title: Pedong and the Tibet road
highlights.text: Damsang fort, stronghold of the Lepcha chief Gaeboo Achyok, the Bhutanese-era Sangchen Dorjee monastery and the 1882 Cross Hill stand within a few kilometres of Pedong, a stage on the wool road from Jelep La to Kalimpong.

highlights.title: Homestay ridges above the Teesta
highlights.text: Sillery Gaon, Icchey Gaon and Ramdhura are small villages with family homestays at ₹1,300–2,200 per person with meals. Walk to Ramitey Dara, where the Teesta is said to make 14 turns below you, and watch dawn reach Kanchenjunga.

getting_there: The railhead is New Jalpaiguri (NJP) and the airport is Bagdogra, both on the edge of Siliguri, about 70 km and 3–3.5 hours from Kalimpong. Shared jeeps leave from the stands near the SNT bus terminus and at Panitanki More when full, ₹200–300 a seat, and arrive at Kalimpong's Motor Stand. NBSTC and private buses run from the Tenzing Norgay bus terminus for about ₹150–200. A reserved car from NJP or Bagdogra costs about ₹3,500–5,000. The usual road is NH10 up the Teesta via Sevoke and Teesta Bazar, which has had repeated landslide and flood closures since October 2023. When it shuts, vehicles go via the Dooars and Gorubathan to Lava, or via Darjeeling and Peshok. Lava, Lolegaon and Rishyap are best reached by reserved car from Kalimpong. Check current status before you travel.
permits: No permits are needed for Kalimpong, Lava, Lolegaon or the Pedong villages, for Indian or foreign visitors. Neora Valley National Park needs an entry permit from the forest department, usually issued at the range office in Lava, plus fees for a vehicle and a compulsory local guide; it closes from mid-June to mid-September. Foreign nationals going on to Sikkim, including the Reshi crossing from Pedong to Rhenock, need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit. Check current status before you travel.
money: On a shoestring, ₹1,300–2,000 a day covers shared jeeps, a simple lodge or homestay with meals, and momos and thalis. A comfortable ₹2,500–4,000 buys a good room in town or a village homestay, a reserved car for the forest villages split between friends, and a guided day in Neora Valley. Comfort trips with Morgan House, private cars every day and paragliding at Deolo run ₹4,000–6,500. People overspend on reserved cars for short hops that a jeep would do, on Puja-week rooms booked late, and on package sightseeing tours that rush ten 'points' in a morning. Village homestays with meals are the best value in the land.

months.weather: Kalimpong 6–15 °C, dry; Lava and Rishyap near freezing at night
months.summary: Cold, dry and often very clear. Kalimpong town is comfortable by day, while Lava, Rishyap and Kolakham are bitter at night and may see snow after a winter storm. Crowds vanish after New Year week and rates drop. The Lepcha New Year, Namsoong, may fall this month. A good month for couples and photographers who pack warm and keep dates loose.
months.tip: Pack a down jacket and ask your homestay for a hot-water bottle; forest villages are well below freezing at night.

months.summary: Still cold, with longer days and clear skies. Losar, the Tibetan New Year, often falls this month, and the monasteries on Durpin and in town fill with butter lamps and families. Snow is possible at Lava and Rishyap early in the month. Prices stay at off-season levels until March, which makes this a cheap, quiet month for monasteries and the Pedong villages.
months.tip: Ask a monastery for the year's Losar date; it follows the Tibetan lunar calendar.

months.summary: Spring. Magnolias and rhododendrons flower in the forests around Lava and Rishyap, the nurseries of Kalimpong are in bloom, and the mornings are still often clear. Birding in Neora Valley picks up as species move uphill. Prices are moderate before the school holidays. A fine month for village homestays and forest walks.
months.tip: Go for viewpoints at dawn; by late March haze often hides the peaks by 10 am.

months.summary: Warm days, flowering forests and the best of the birding season in Neora Valley and around Lava and Kolakham. Kanchenjunga shows early in the morning before haze rises. Teesta rafting usually runs in the dry weeks. Late in the month the plains' school holidays start and rooms in town fill up. A good month for nature lovers.
months.tip: Book Neora Valley guides at the Lava forest office a day ahead in April.

months.summary: Peak season for families from the plains, especially in Kalimpong town and Lava. Afternoon showers begin, and views are often hidden by midday. The higher villages stay pleasant when the plains are hot: Rishyap, Charkhole and Lolegaon are cool at night. Book ahead for weekends, and watch for the first landslides late in the month.
months.tip: Pick a ridge village over town in May; it is cooler and less crowded.

months.summary: The monsoon usually arrives by mid-June. Neora Valley National Park closes from mid-June to mid-September, rafting stops, and NH10 along the Teesta becomes prone to slides and closures, as it has been every year since the 2023 flood. Early June can still work for Kalimpong town. After that, travel only with flexible dates.
months.tip: Keep a buffer day before any train or flight; NH10 closures can last days.

months.summary: The wettest stretch of the year. Landslides block roads for hours or days, views are rare, and leeches are out on forest paths. Rooms are cheap and the hills are deep green. If you come, stay in Kalimpong town, enjoy the monasteries, nurseries and cafés, and avoid the forest villages, whose roads suffer most.
months.tip: Check road status with your hotel each morning before any day trip.

months.summary: Much like July: heavy rain, slides and short clear spells. Neora Valley stays closed and rafting does not run. Hotels offer their lowest rates. Kalimpong town works for a quiet, rainy stay with books and good food, but long road journeys are a gamble. Monitor NH10 and the Gorubathan road closely.
months.tip: Pack leech socks and a proper raincoat if you plan even short walks.

months.summary: The rain eases through the month, and the last week can bring the first clear mornings. Neora Valley usually reopens in mid or late September. Prices stay low until the Puja holidays, which in some years begin late in the month and bring the autumn rush. A good month for value if you travel late and can wait out a wet day.
months.tip: If Durga Puja falls in late September, book rooms before the month begins.

months.summary: The clear season begins. The air is washed after the monsoon and Kanchenjunga stands on the skyline most mornings. Dashain and Durga Puja, then Tihar, fill the hills with families and with festival life. Book rooms, jeeps and homestays well ahead for the holiday weeks. Rafting at Teesta Bazar usually restarts when the river drops.
months.tip: Book October holiday weeks a month or more in advance, especially in Lava and Lolegaon.

months.summary: Our favourite month. Puja crowds have gone, rates settle and the mountains are clear most mornings. Tihar falls early in the month in some years. Neora Valley is open and quiet, and the ridge villages at Charkhole, Icchey Gaon and Ramdhura give their best dawns. Evenings are cold, so pack warm layers.
months.tip: Pack warm: November nights fall to about 5 °C in Lava and colder in Rishyap.

months.summary: Cold, clear and mostly calm until the Christmas and New Year week, when town hotels fill. On 20 December Lepchas gather at Damsang fort near Pedong for Gaeboo Achyok's birth anniversary, and Namsoong, the Lepcha New Year, may fall late in the month. Kalimpong's churches hold Christmas services. Early December is one of the best windows for views.
months.tip: Come in the first half of December for clear views at off-season prices.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Two nights in Kalimpong town covers Durpin and Zang Dhok Palri, Thongsa Gompa, a nursery, Dr Graham's Homes and Deolo, and the haat if your dates fit. Add two nights in Lava or Lolegaon for forests and Neora Valley, or two in Sillery Gaon or Icchey Gaon for village life. Five to six nights is a relaxed trip.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to reach Kalimpong from NJP?
faqs.a: A shared jeep from the SNT stand or Panitanki More in Siliguri, ₹200–300 a seat and 3–3.5 hours, or an NBSTC or private bus from the Tenzing Norgay terminus for about ₹150–200. Take an auto from NJP to the stand first. NH10 has had closures since October 2023, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Kalimpong?
faqs.a: October to mid-December gives the clearest views of Kanchenjunga, with November the steadiest month. March to May brings flowers, birds and warm days but more haze. December to February is cold and clear, with a chance of snow at Lava and Rishyap. June to September is the monsoon, with landslides and Neora Valley closed.

It is different. Kalimpong is smaller, warmer, quieter and cheaper, with monasteries, nurseries and a strong Lepcha and Tibetan history, but no toy train and fewer big-name sights. Its villages, Lava, Lolegaon, Rishyap and Sillery Gaon, are the real draw. Many travellers do both, a day apart by shared jeep.

faqs.q: How much does a Kalimpong trip cost per day?
faqs.a: About ₹1,300–2,000 a day on a shoestring with shared jeeps, simple rooms and local food; ₹2,500–4,000 with a good room or homestay with meals and shared reserved cars; ₹4,000–6,500 for comfort with Morgan House and private cars. Prices are indicative for 2025–26 and rise in Puja and New Year weeks.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Kalimpong or Lava?
faqs.a: No. Indian and foreign visitors need no permit for Kalimpong, Lava, Lolegaon or the Pedong villages. Neora Valley National Park requires an entry permit and a local guide from the forest office at Lava, and it closes mid-June to mid-September. Foreigners going on to Sikkim need a Restricted Area Permit.

NH10, the main road from Siliguri up the Teesta, has had repeated landslide and flood closures since the October 2023 Teesta flood, mostly in the monsoon. When it closes, vehicles come via the Dooars, Gorubathan and Lava, or via Darjeeling and Peshok, adding 1–3 hours. Ask at the jeep stand and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which village near Kalimpong is best for a homestay?
faqs.a: For Kanchenjunga dawns and walks, Sillery Gaon or Icchey Gaon near Pedong. For forest and birds, Kolakham or Rishyap near Lava. For old woods and quiet, Charkhole or Lolegaon. Homestays charge about ₹1,300–2,200 per person with dinner and breakfast. Most need a car from Kalimpong, Lava or Pedong.

faqs.q: Can I see red pandas in Neora Valley?
faqs.a: Possibly, but sightings are rare and never promised. Red pandas live in the park's higher forests, around Rachela and above 2,500 m, and are most often seen early on quiet winter and spring mornings with a good local guide. Book the guide at the Lava forest office and keep expectations modest.

to_confirm: Exact Neora Valley entry, vehicle and guide fees for 2025–26 are set by the forest department and change; we give ranges.
Teesta rafting operations after the 2023 flood vary season to season; confirm locally.
